title: Microsoft Outlook Is Down
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson

        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Microsoft Outlook is down for many users as of Monday afternoon.
                                            Downdetector highlights tens of thousands of users reports suggesting issues with Outlook.
                                            In addition, other Microsoft services, including Microsoft 365, are also down.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're trying to check your inbox or send an email in Microsoft Outlook, only to find the app uncooperative, you're not alone. Outlook is currently down for many users as of Monday afternoon. That's apparent to anyone who can't get the app to work: Downdetector, which highlights user reports for app outages, shows tens of thousands of reports as of 3:00 p.m. ET, and while the rate of reports does seem to be decreasing, thousands of reports keep coming in with every refresh.  As CNET reports, Microsoft has officially confirmed the outage itself. The company posted on its Microsoft 365 Status X account, stating: “We’ve identified an issue with an authentication component which is contributing to impact. To address this, we’ve developed a remediation strategy, and we’re applying it to a portion of infrastructure to test its efficacy. Once we’ve confirmed this resolves impact, we’ll apply the solution more broadly. For more information, please see EX1464935 in the admin center.”As such, the company should be rolling out a fix in due time, though it's difficult to say how long that may be. Recent outages have been fixed in a matter of hours, while others have stretched into the following day. At the time of writing, Downdetector shows that 38% of users are reporting issues receiving messages in Outlook, while 24% report issues with the app, and 21% with logging in. 
As it happens, Outlook isn't the only Microsoft product facing issues: Users report that Microsoft Teams, Microsoft Store, Microsoft Azur  and Microsoft 365 in general are experiencing  issues. In addition, OpenAI users are reporting issues with ChatGPT. 
            
                What do you think so far?

Joel Cunningham
                            
        
            Joel Cunningham
                
                                            Deputy Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJoel Cunningham is Lifehacker’s Deputy Editor. He has 15 years of experience as a writer and editor. Previously, he was managing editor of content marketing for Barnes & Noble, where he founded the Barnes & Noble Sci-Fi & Fantasy Blog.

            Credit: NurPhoto / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Update: As of 5 p.m. EDT, the problem seems to have largely been resolved, as reports on Downdetector have dropped from a high of around 10,000 to under 500. Twitch still has not commented on the issue beyond its initial status message.If you're having some trouble logging into Twitch for a gaming session right now, it's not just you: According to Downdetector, thousands of users are reporting issues with the online gaming platform. It looks like the problems began around 2:30 p.m. EDT, when reports of access issues started to trickle in. By around 4 p.m., those numbers spiked to almost 10,000 and remain elevated as of this writing. Twitch has yet to reveal what might be causing the problem or offer a timeframe for a fix, with its status page merely sharing the following:
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Service Negatively Impacted: We have received reports of impacted services. This could manifest in chat not working, login difficulties, search impaired, etc. We're looking into the issue.No additional updates have been shared on the company's social media profiles, including X. According to Twitch, the platform experienced its last major outage two years ago, in August 2024.

title: These Five New Features Are Coming to Android Devices
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 3, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Google
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Google's September Android drop comes with five new features for Android devices.
                                            Google is rolling out a new feature that lets you keep tabs on your stuff without using a tracker.
                                            The company is also rolling out its own take on Apple's "Vehicle Motion Cues" to prevent motion sickness.
                                            Google Messages users are getting new chat customization features, as well as Google Keep integration.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Another month, another "Drop." Google announced its latest crop of features for Android devices this week, all coming as part of its September Android Drop. While the list is relatively small, these five new features all actually seem pretty useful. In fact, with this update, Google is kind of making the case to avoid buying one of its newest products. 
Keeps tabs on your stuff without using a trackerGoogle is funny. The company finally rolls out its own competitor to the AirTag, the Pixel Tag, then immediately undercuts it with a new Find Hub feature. "Soon," Google says, you'll have the ability to ask Gemini to remember where you put your stuff, making it possible to keep tabs on those items without needing a dedicated tracker. Google says the feature is for "things you don't put a tracker tag on," like, perhaps, your passport or a spare key, but there aren't any rules here. You can simply ask Gemini to remember that you put your keys in your bedside drawer, and it'll store that location for you. You can even choose to add a photo if you want the extra assistance. When you can't find something, you can ask Gemini where it is, or check the new "remembered items" tab in Find Hub. Google doesn't have a specific timeline for when this feature will roll out, but it does say that it'll work with Android 16 and newer in countries that support both Gemini and Find Hub.
Android is getting its own anti-motion sickness featureWith iOS 18, Apple introduced "Vehicle Motion Cues," a feature that aims to reduce motion sickness by placing a series of dots on your screen. As the vehicle moves, so do the dots. That way, your brain doesn't get "confused" by looking at a stationary screen in a moving vehicle; it thinks the screen is moving as well, hopefully keeping your senses in equilibrium. While developers brought this concept to Android devices through third-party apps, Google now has a version of the feature of its own. Google's take is called "Motion Assist," and it works just about the same way as Apple's. Like Vehicle Motion Cues, you can customize how these dots actually look; in this case, you can control their shape, color, and opacity. You can choose to have the feature kick on automatically, or pin it as a Quick Setting tile to access it whenever you want. Google says this feature is coming to all phones running Android 17.    "Guided vision" is coming to Gemini LiveJust about every tech company with an AI platform offers a "Live" feature, which lets the AI "see" through your device's camera to help answer questions about your surroundings. For Google, that's Gemini Live. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Now, Google is adding "Guided vision" to Gemini Live, a feature designed for blind and low-vision users. Guided vision uses Gemini Live to help you navigate your surroundings in a more accessible way: Rather than simply answering questions about "what type of plant is this" or "when was this building built," Google says Guided vision can help with reading fine print on a nutrition label, or discerning the different dishes on a menu in a restaurant with low light. Furthermore, Guided vision can help you line up your camera if you aren't pointing it in the right spot. This feature is actually coming to a larger number of devices than some other features, as Google says you'll be able to use it with Android 9 and newer devices where Gemini is available.  Google Messages now has collaborative Google Keep integrationIf you have a friend or a group chat that frequently collaborates on lists (think grocery lists or vacation planning), Google Messages is getting a helpful upgrade. Following this Pixel Drop, Google Messages users will notice a new Google Keep icon in the (+) menu. Once activated, you'll be able to create and edit new notes directly in your chats. Rather than jumping between Google Keep and Google Messages, you can chat and collaborate in one app. As someone on the iOS side of things, I hope Apple—ahem—takes notes here. Google Messages gets new chat customizations Google Messages is also getting some new chat customization options. Now, you can change the background of a chat to whatever you want, including photos from your library. When you do, the text bubbles automatically change to match that image's color scheme. That said, you can adjust the colors to whatever you like, or customize the bubbles without changing the background.

title: Here's How AI Watermarks Work (and How to Properly Check for One)
description:
Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: René Ramos/Lifehacker/OpenAI/Claude/Google/Getty Images
body:
Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: René Ramos/Lifehacker/OpenAI/Claude/Google/Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Recently, Anthropic announced that its Claude models will soon begin marking its text output with invisible watermarks. At the same time, Google revealed that its own visible Gemini watermark on generated images will now be optional. These are just two contradictory examples of the wildly varied methods of watermarking AI output. So, let’s break down how AI watermarks work, and how you can detect them even when they're "invisible."How does AI watermarking work?The exact method for watermarking AI output will depend on the type of media being generated, but the principle is generally the same: The generated media is embedded with data that is undetectable (or occasionally detectable) to the human eye or ear, but which identifies it as AI-produced. Watermark-detecting tools can then be used to identify if something was made with AI, without guessing or using an unreliable AI “detector”. Here are some examples of how watermarks may be implemented for various media types.For images: Since the pixels of an image are mathematical values, they can be slightly modified to embed a digital signature, without perceptible changes to the image itself. Google’s SynthID, for example, distributes an invisible signature across any generated image, so even a cropped version will still contain detectable portions of the watermark. Note: This is distinct from the visible gray symbol in the corner of Gemini images. Even if you turn off the visible Gemini watermark, the invisible one remains.For audio: Embedding a watermark in audio files can be even easier, placing signature sounds outside the range of human hearing (typically below 20Hz or above 20,000Hz). SynthID has an audio component that can be heard by watermark detectors, but remains imperceptible to the ear.For video: Naturally, generated video tends to use a combination of both of the above watermarking methods, though it’s worth keeping in mind that someone making fake content could, for example, generate AI audio to accompany real video, meaning the watermark might appear in one piece of the content, but not another.For text: Every next word an LLM generates comes with a probability score. The sentence “The cat is” could end with “fluffy,” “cute,” or “small.” Each one of those words is given a percentage likelihood that it will appear. Text watermarks work by inflating the chances that certain sets of random words will appear. This can make it possible to detect LLM-generated text without changing its semantic meaning. However, this tends to work better for longer pieces of text, which provides more chances to detect the presence of less-likely words.For metadata: While not strictly a watermark, C2PA is a framework for adding metadata that can help verify the origin of a piece of media. Some camera manufacturers, for example, have implemented C2PA to give photographers a traceable record of where an image came from. This can also include noting whether an image was generated with AI tools.While SynthID originated with Google’s DeepMind, the company open-sourced the protocol, and now it’s also used by other AI companies, including OpenAI. Some companies. conversely, do not use a watermark at all—and among those that do, the implementation can be inconsistent between tools. In other words, the presence of an AI watermark can confirm something was made or modified with AI, but the absence of one can’t prove it wasn’t.
How can you detect AI watermarks?Despite SynthID and C2PA being relatively common, it’s still kind of a crapshoot to properly detect the presence of watermarks or metadata that will confirm if a piece of media was generated with AI. OpenAI has a standalone tool to check for SynthID or C2PA in a file, and Google lets you access its verification tools via Gemini or, with the right prompting, directly via Google itself.However, these tools have limitations. OpenAI’s detector, for some reason, only seems to detect media generated by OpenAI itself. During my testing, I tried uploading images generated via Gemini—which could detect its own SynthID watermark—and OpenAI’s tool did not find it.Meanwhile, Google created a SynthID Detector portal, but it’s currently available on an invite-only basis, specifically for journalists and verification professionals. You can still access some SynthID detection functions via Gemini or Google, though in some cases, you’ll need the right prompts to do so. In my testing, when asking “is this real” for a known AI-generated image via Gemini, the tool invoked a verification tool to check for SynthID. However, when doing the same process via Google, the LLM’s output resembled a visual analysis instead. It only invoked a SynthID check when specifically asked to do so.Even if you do your diligence to check for every version of a SynthID watermark or C2PA metadata, it’s still possible that a piece of media could have some other form of watermark that requires a different detector. Unfortunately, unless you have a strong indicator of which tool was used to create a piece of generated media, it can still be difficult to thoroughly check for every kind of watermark.When it comes to text-based watermarks like the kind Claude or even Gemini use, detecting them can still be very difficult. For starters, neither offers a public way to check for the text watermark just yet (Google's SynthID Detector portal can do so, but it's not generally available). Can AI watermarking be circumvented?With enough work, any watermark can technically be removed, though SynthID specifically is pretty resistant to most typical forms of modification. An AI-generated image with a SynthID watermark that has been cropped, filtered, or modified can still retain enough of its original watermark to be detectable. It’s not impossible to remove, but it’s generally hard to do so accidentally.Removing metadata like C2PA, on the other hand, is considerably easier. For images, that’s as simple as taking a screenshot. A screenshot of an image essentially creates a new image file based on the pixels visible on the screen. This means that any watermark that affects those pixels can remain, but an entirely new set of metadata is created, wiping any C2PA data along with it.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
That means that if you want to maintain a metadata chain that lets you prove the authenticity of an image, it’s important to download or upload the specific original files and make sure any editing tools you use support maintaining that metadata.Text watermarks are among the easiest to get around. Since they work by simply altering the probability that certain words will appear, running text through another AI tool that rephrases the words without using a watermark, or even manually rewriting a block of text, can potentially remove the watermark.It’s important to keep in mind that a watermark can be added to an authentic piece of media. If someone uploads an authentic photo to a tool like Gemini to perform simple edits, the output image will have a SynthID watermark, too. This doesn’t mean the whole image is inauthentic, but it will still be flagged by watermark detectors.Similarly, it’s possible to generate an image of a subject, cut the subject out, and add it to an image using traditional manipulation techniques like Photoshop to create an inauthentic image that’s mostly made from an authentic image. Whether or not the watermark will remain on the portion of an image that was AI-generated can only be determined on a case-by-case basis.As mentioned before, the absence of a watermark cannot prove that an image is authentic. Even the presence of a watermark can’t prove that the substance of an image isn’t real. Watermarks and metadata are simply tools to help you figure out where a piece of media likely came from and how it might’ve been modified. Ultimately, it’s still up to you to verify the things you see and hear online.

title: Strava Is Now Forcing Premium Users to See Its AI Workout Summaries (Whether They Want to or Not)
body:
Beth Skwarecki
                            
        
            Beth Skwarecki
                
                                            Senior Health Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceBeth Skwarecki is Lifehacker’s Senior Health Editor, and holds certifications as a personal trainer and weightlifting coach. She has been writing about health for over 10 years.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 28, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Meredith Dietz, Beth Skwarecki, Strava
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Strava's "Athlete Intelligence" offers AI summaries to subscribers, who used to be able to opt out.
                                            Premium users can no longer turn off Athlete Intelligence.
                                            Strava confirmed that they took away the opt-out, but declined to say when.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        You can’t turn off Strava’s AI summaries anymore. Sometime in July or August, the feature, called “Athlete Intelligence,” became a built-in part of premium subscriptions. If you have a free account, you still won’t see it, but if you subscribe to Strava Premium, you’ll now have the summaries stuck onto all of your workouts. What is Strava's "Athlete Intelligence"?Athlete Intelligence, conveniently abbreviated AI, is a Strava feature that gives text responses to your workouts. It’s only available for premium subscribers. Strava refers to “insights” in these responses, but as far as I can tell, they just seem to regurgitate the information from the workout description, sometimes with added errors. I used the feature briefly, around the time it launched (I was a premium subscriber then), but quickly turned it off when I realized it wasn’t telling me anything interesting. I asked my colleague Meredith Dietz, who has a premium subscription, whether she had seen anything useful in her Athlete Intelligence. She said, “They’re usually positive, so that’s nice. But ultimately: useless.” 
Meredith has written more about why AI fitness summaries are mostly useless, and Strava’s AI checks every box: it doesn’t use enough context to understand what’s going on, it presents generic advice as if it were personal, and it’s overconfident in its incomplete data. She showed me a recent Athlete Intelligence summary that said a run was both a “recovery run” and included her “fastest pace in two weeks.” Those are simply not compatible statements. Another message complimented her “solid half-marathon effort” on a run that Meredith says was “not even close to a half-marathon effort.” What happened behind the scenes? You used to be able to turn off the AI. When Strava launched Athlete Intelligence in October 2024, it was a “beta” feature available to premium users only. Since then—as far as I can remember—Strava’s support page had instructions for opting out of Athlete Intelligence. But that changed recently. The last Wayback Machine snapshot that included those instructions is from June 30, 2026. A snapshot from Aug. 4 removed both the question and answer about opting out. On Aug. 26, I noticed a Reddit thread where users were wondering where the opt-out feature went. The support page currently says, “There isn’t an option to opt out of Athlete Intelligence.” I asked what happened, and received an answer from a Strava spokesperson: “As was standard practice for experimental features, Athlete Intelligence launched with a "turn off" mechanism scoped to its initial beta period. Given the feature’s formal exit from beta, that mechanism is no longer available. We invite all subscribers to tap Give Feedback to help us improve the insights they see.”
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Athlete Intelligence officially left beta in February of last year. If the support page was kept up to date over the subsequent year and a half, then it seems the opt-out was removed much later. (The instructions used to say to click “leave beta” and then changed to “leave Athlete Intelligence” sometime before June 21 this year.) I asked Strava for clarification on the timeline, and got the answer: “Thanks for the follow up, we're not able to provide additional information.”Why “Athlete Intelligence” has been such a disappointmentStrava claimed in its February 2025 announcement that over 80% of users found Athlete Intelligence useful. That seems hard to believe, given the weaknesses that both Meredith and I noticed in our own AI summaries. For all my browsing of Strava user forums, I’ve often seen people complaining about the AI’s tone or pointing out its mistakes; I’m really not seeing anyone praising it for being insightful or for helping to analyze or plan training. Meredith finds the summaries easy to ignore. I found they annoyed me, so I hid them while it was still possible to do so. So far I’m not seeing anybody who opted out complaining that the summaries are back; it’s possible they will remain hidden. But the option to turn them off is no longer available. You can still “leave feedback” on a given response, but there used to be an option to leave Athlete Intelligence altogether. That option is no longer there, and given Strava’s statement, it doesn’t seem likely it will come back.

title: Here's When GrapheneOS Is Coming to Motorola Phones
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 24, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Angel Garcia/Bloomberg via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            GrapheneOS is working with Motorola to bring the privacy and security OS to more smartphones.
                                            The company shared updates in its partnership, announcing that Motorola's 2027 lineup would be the first to receive support.
                                            GrapheneOS says that these will be Motorola's first phones that meet all security requirements, though the company will only support its "slab" phones at first.
                                            GrapheneOS is also working on adding support for Motorola's foldable and flippable phones, as well as the 11th-generation Pixel devices.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Many of us don't think twice about the OS our smartphones are running. On the surface, it really seems like there are only two options: iOS, for those of us with iPhones, and Android, for all other phones. But the conversation is much more nuanced than that: Many non-Apple smartphone manufacturers have their own takes on Android that make for a slightly different experience. Samsung has One UI, OnePlus (RIP) has OxygenOS, and Nothing has Nothing OS, for example. (Pixel ships with stock Android, as Google makes both the hardware and the software.)However, the mobile OS rabbit hole goes even deeper. If you're particularly technical (and you don't have an iPhone) you can install a new OS on your smartphone to give you added control or features you won't find on Android. GrapheneOS just so happens to be one of those custom OSes, and its list of supported devices is about to grow.GrapheneOS is an open-source mobile OS designed with privacy and security in mind. While the OS is built on the Android Open Source Project, it employs a number of privacy and security features to both thwart common security vulnerabilities and block invasive trackers from scraping your data. Because it's built on Android, it supports Android apps, but won't include Google apps or services by default. It won't block Google Play outright, however: Users can choose to install Google Play in a "sandbox," which limits the elements of your phone Google's apps and services can access.   
Crucially, GrapheneOS has a long list of requirements manufacturers must meet before it decides to support new devices. Some of those key prerequisites include the ability to run alternate OSes with full hardware security access, commitments for at least five years of updates, secure element integration, and hardware memory tagging, among many others. If you want to run this custom OS that prioritizes privacy and security, you either need to pick your new smartphone carefully, or hope your preferred manufacturer creates a device in the future that meets these specifications.  GrapheneOS is coming to Motorola phones next yearAs of this article, only Google's Pixel phones currently support GrapheneOS—though GrapheneOS doesn't necessarily recommend using all supported Pixels at this time. The OS will run on Pixel 6 and newer (minus Pixel 11) but GrapheneOS recommends at least Pixel 8 or newer, because of Google's minimum seven years support, and Pixel 8's hardware memory tagging.  
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
However, Pixels won't be the exclusive choice for GrapheneOS for long. The OS maker has been working with Motorola to bring support to its phones. And, as reported by The Verge, GrapheneOS recently announced some key updates on this front. Of note, Motorola's 2027 lineup of "slab" phones (non-folding, in other words) are currently planned to be the first to support GrapheneOS, which should support Qualcomm's upcoming Snapdragon 8 Elite chips. GrapheneOS explained its thought process in a Mastodon thread: It says that Motorola's current-generation phones, including the Motorola Signature, Razr Fold, and Razr Ultra, "are very close" to meeting its aforementioned security requirements, but are missing some crucial features coming to Motorola's 2027 lineup, including adequate secure element integration. GrapheneOS also emphasizes its enthusiasm for Snapdragon chips, which it says provide better CPU and GPU performance as well as isolated components (such as cellular, wifi, Bluetooth), over Google's proprietary Tensor chip. GrapheneOS says that Tensor has been a "sidegrade or downgrade" from Snapdragon in many ways, but came with security advantages that Snapdragon hasn't caught up to yet—though that now appears to be changing. While GrapheneOS has found it harder to work with Pixel in recent years, the company says that Motorola has done much of the work in bringing GrapheneOS to its devices, which is encouraging: My guess is users who choose to install GrapheneOS should find it well-optimized.GrapheneOS says it plans to support Motorola's foldable and flippable phones as well. The company says that it already supports the Pixel Fold, Pixel 9 Pro Fold, and Pixel 10 Pro Fold, so the foldable form factor is nothing new. However, a "flip" phone is a new design for the company. In addition, GrapheneOS is working on support for the 11th-generation Pixel devices.

title: These Google Maps and Apple Maps Alternatives Still Call It ‘Lake Ontario’ (for Now)
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise

        September 2, 2026

        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Jim WATSON / AFP via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Following Trump's executive order, Google Maps and Apple Maps have renamed Lake Ontario "Lake America."
                                            Google says it follows the U.S. Geographic Names Information System, and has updated its map accordingly.
                                            Trump directly appealed to Apple, on the other hand, to change the name on its map.
                                            Some other navigation apps have not changed Lake Ontario's name—at least, not yet.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Last week, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America." The move was retaliation against Canada for walking away from contentious trade talks and in spite of the fact that Lake Ontario's name has nothing to do with the Canadian province. Regardless, tech companies are now dealing with the consequences.Why did Google Maps change Lake Ontario's name?If you live in the U.S., you may have opened Google Maps this past weekend to see that the app had already changed Lake Ontario's name. Even if you don't live in the U.S., you may see the name change: As it happens, there are now three different naming schemes for the lake in Google's navigation app. If you use the app in the U.S., you'll see "Lake America." If you use it in Canada, you'll see "Lake Ontario." If you use it anywhere else in the world, you'll see "Lake Ontario (Lake America)." Thanks, Google.
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Google
                    
    
Google did the same when Trump "changed" the name of the Gulf of Mexico to "Gulf of America." While Google explains in a blog post that its policy is to follow the naming conventions of the U.S. Geographic Names Information System, it's also arguable that the company doesn't want to get into hot water with the Trump Administration, lest it be punished with future policies that could hurt its trillion-dollar business. Now, Apple Maps is in the same boat. While Apple's app kept "Lake Ontario" on its map longer than Google, it has since changed the name as well. Trump reportedly urged Apple directly to make the switch. (Like Google, the company previously changed the Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America as well.) 
Whether you consider it basic bureaucratic compliance or corporate cowardice, Google Maps and Apple Maps now call the lake by its "new" name. It doesn't affect how the apps work (maybe unless you're looking for directions to, or information about, Lake Ontario), but if the change rankles you, you have other options: As it stands, there are now two key alternatives that still label it "Lake Ontario."As of this writing, only a couple of apps available to download call Lake Ontario by its official/"former" name. Whether that will remain true as the week goes on remains a question, but for now, the following apps are still reflecting the global consensus:
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
MapQuestOrganic MapsTechnically, Waze also still calls it Lake Ontario on its map, and the name pops up when you start to search for it. But once you tap the result, the app then swaps the name to Lake America. That's to be expected, given Google owns Waze, but the app initially tricked me into thinking it had maintained the previous status quo.Will other apps change Lake Ontario's name?Will these apps maintain the Lake Ontario name over the long term? When I first published this article, Apple hadn't changed the name, but I had expected them to. As I said above, Apple ultimately changed the Gulf of Mexico's name, so it followed that it would likely do the same with the lake. However, MapQuest and Organic Maps still call the Gulf of Mexico by its correct name, so chances are good they'll keep Lake Ontario on their maps for the foreseeable future.

title: Here's How to Protect Your Privacy If Someone Is Recording You With Their Glasses
description:

body:
We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
        
        Meta’s smart glasses are earning a reputation for being a privacy nightmare—to put it mildly. While the company is taking steps to make it harder to record people without their knowledge, it’s still not possible to prevent being recorded. So, what can you do if you think someone is using their glasses to record you without your consent?
Know your rights if someone is recording youKnowing whether or not someone is legally allowed to record you won’t necessarily protect you from being recorded, but it’s a solid foundation to start with. And determining whether someone can record you generally boils down to two basic questions: Do you have a reasonable expectation of privacy? And do you live in a one- or two-party consent state?In the United States, a reasonable expectation of privacy is a legal principle that can help determine whether you have a right not to be recorded (in other jurisdictions, this concept may have a different name or criteria). The classic example of this would be standing outside on the street, but pointing a camera inside a person’s window. Even though the person recording outside is technically “in public,” the subject being recorded has a reasonable expectation that being inside their home entitles them to privacy—yes, even if the window is open.
When it comes to smart glasses, this principle applies as it would with any other camera. If someone tries to record you in a place where you have a reasonable expectation of privacy—your home, hotel room, or a bathroom, for example—then they are legally in the wrong.Within places that have a reasonable expectation of privacy, some places in the U.S. require that both parties to a conversation consent to it being recorded, while others require only one party to consent. The key here is that in all cases, the person recording must be a participant in the conversation. A third party listening in by pointing a camera or a microphone at you never has a right to record you in a place where you can reasonably expect privacy.This also means that even if the person wearing smart glasses is part of the conversation, recording you still might be illegal if you’re in a two-party consent state. Obviously, none of this applies when you’re in public places, or even on private property that’s open to the public like a restaurant or store, but it’s usually worth knowing your rights.Just because you have a legal right to privacy doesn’t mean you can prevent someone from recording you, but it can put you in a better position to have footage of you taken down or taking legal action against it in the future. And if you control the space where someone is recording you—say, inside your own home—you can always have them removed.Appeal to private authoritiesYour legal rights only matter so much in the moment if you’re faced with someone who won’t take no for an answer. Take this incident earlier this year, where a man filmed himself accosting British comedian Diane Morgan in the middle of a shoot. While the film crew in this instance obviously didn’t have a legal right to privacy, and probably did not have a legal right to remove the intruder, the person filming also clearly wasn’t deterred by potentially incurring a harassment charge. So, what can you do if someone simply won’t relent?In public-accessible spaces, your best bet is likely to find whoever owns or manages the space you’re in. You might not have the ability to stop someone from recording you inside a Starbucks, but the manager can kick them out if they’re causing a problem. Some places and organizations have started banning the use of recording-capable glasses altogether—so it's worth familiarizing yourself with the policies of the local businesses where you hang out. If you think someone’s recording you in public, it can be helpful to know if there’s a local bar or bookstore that bans these glasses. Even if it’s just to have a place to duck into if someone is recording you nearby, or to know who to ask for help to get someone to stop bothering you.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
More tips to prevent being recordedGetting someone to stop recording or observing you entirely is the ideal, but if that’s not an option, you might have to resort to some more creative solutions. Including, but not limited to the following:Try the Nearby Glasses app. This open-source application is available for Android and iOS, and can potentially identify nearby smart glasses. It uses Bluetooth data from nearby devices to try to determine if any smart glasses are in your vicinity. It’s not 100% reliable, but it can be a helpful indicator. It should also go without saying, but knowing that someone nearby has smart glasses doesn’t mean you know who is wearing them. So be careful before approaching someone that you’re not sure is wearing them.Watch for signs of tampering on the notification LED. Meta’s smart glasses are supposed to have an LED that alerts people around the user that a recording is in progress. A recent update is supposed to ensure that recording will cease if the LED is covered, but it’s still possible to tamper with the glasses to prevent this. It’s not great if someone is recording you without your permission, but if you see someone who appears to have visibly modified their smart glasses to prevent people from noticing the recording, then it’s extra important to take action.Don’t bother playing Disney music. One common tip you’ll find is to play copyrighted music from a particularly litigious company. The idea here is that, if the offending recorder tries to upload the footage to a site like YouTube or TikTok, then it could potentially get removed on copyright grounds.This isn’t really how those platforms often work. Content can get taken down due to a copyright claim, but just as often it can either get demonetized or simply muted. And in those cases, the copyright system isn’t really going to help you. Playing music to drown out a conversation might not hurt, but it’s better to rely on your own privacy complaints to take down videos, rather than hoping Disney will save you.

title: This Is the Best Ad-Free Alternative to Apple Maps
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 26, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Prykhodov via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple Maps officially launched ads in search this week.
                                            You'll see ads in the new "Suggested Places" field, as well as in Apple Maps search results.
                                            You can't block Apple Maps ads, but you can choose an alternative that skips out on them completely.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        This week, Apple Maps officially launched ads in search. It's not necessarily a surprise, mind you: We learned back in October that Apple planned to roll out ads at some point. But it's still a bit jarring to see Apple actually commit to the plan. Now, most of the mainstream navigation apps come with ads, which makes getting around without dealing with ads difficult—but not impossible.How Apple Maps' ads work Once ads hit your app, you'll start seeing them when you search for new destinations. That includes both in the new "Suggested Places" section, as well as within search results as well. Like other platforms that float sponsored items to the top of search results, you'll likely want to be a bit more scrupulous, since the top pick might not actually be the most relevant to your query. What's more, there's no way to actually disable these ads. There are ad blockers for iPhone, but they're limited, and won't block Apple's own ads. As such, it just doesn't feel very "Apple" to deal with ads on the company's own navigation app—especially if you're already giving Apple money every month. While Apple Maps doesn't have a paid subscription, Apple offers plenty of services at a cost. As YouTuber Quinn Nelson notes, some users are paying $50 per month for Apple One, and still having to deal with ads on Apple Maps. Of course, it's the same story for Google Maps: Google's famous navigation app also has mandatory ads, whether you subscribe to one of Google's services or not. In Apple's view, its approach is better than competitors like Google, as the company is adamant its ads preserve your privacy. But even if that's the case, I'm not sure it's going to sell users on the new approach.
It's tough to find a good navigation alternative to Apple Maps or Google Maps. That includes Waze, which is also owned by Google and also has ads. However, there is one solid—albeit rather underground—choice for anyone whose top priority is a lack of ads.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Organic Maps is a free and open-source app that prioritizes privacy for navigation. According to the developer, the app works entirely offline, and does not track people as they use it. (How refreshing.) As such, you could download your maps, disable cellular services, and still have the ability to navigate—of course, you can use it while connected, as well. The app supports a number of features that you'll find on other more mainstream platforms, including cycling and hiking routes, turn-by-turn directions, public transit maps, and dark mode. Organic Maps uses OpenStreetMap to provide its navigation data. While the benefit of OpenStreetMap is that it's also open-source, so users all over the globe can add their own data points, it likely isn't as robust as Apple's map data, not to mention Google's decades of data. Still, users have generally positive reviews on the iOS App Store, suggesting that OpenStreetMap's data offers an adequate alternative to Apple Maps. Now, if you're used to scrolling through restaurant reviews or checking out Street View, you'll miss that here. While Organic Maps does have a search function, it's lacking compared to other platforms. This is definitely a navigation-first app, rather than a full Apple Maps or Google Maps replacement. Still, if you're looking for an ad-free alternative, there are few better options out there at this time.

And some of its smarter tracking features also depend on the phone, app, and shooting mode you're using, so the experience isn't identical across every device.     Table of Contents
    
        
        Amazon’s early Labor Day 2026 sale has dropped the Blink Battery Doorbell 2K+ and Mini 2K+ bundle to $69.98 from $119.98, a discount of 42%. According to price trackers, that’s also the lowest price the bundle has reached so far. It’s a practical pairing if you want coverage at the front door and somewhere inside the house without buying two separate systems. The battery-powered doorbell can keep an eye on visitors and packages outside, while the Mini 2K+ works well for a hallway, living room, pet area, or anywhere else you want an indoor view.
The doorbell is built around a 2K, head-to-toe view, so you’re more likely to catch both a visitor’s face and a package left near the ground in the same frame. Two-way audio also gives you a way to respond when you’re elsewhere in the house or away from home. In its review of the Blink Battery Doorbell 2K+, PCMag specifically highlighted the improved resolution and broader framing. The Mini 2K+ also holds up well on its own: PCMag found the video sharp enough to call the camera an excellent value—it can also double as an indoor chime for the doorbell, so you’ll still hear when someone rings even if your phone isn’t nearby.That said, while live view, motion alerts, and two-way talk work without a monthly fee, cloud recording and advanced detection features require a Blink subscription (starting at $3.99 per month for the Basic plan, which covers one device). The included Sync Module Core also doesn’t give you local storage by itself, although local recording is available with compatible hardware and a MicroSD card sold separately. That makes this bundle a better fit for someone who wants inexpensive coverage at the door and inside the home than for someone specifically trying to build a subscription-free security setup.You can find more deals worth considering from Amazon and other retailers in our ongoing Labor Day coverage across tech, home, and other categories.Amazon Labor Day Deals FAQsWhen do Labor Day sales start?Early Labor Day sales have already started. More retailers are likely to start their own sales leading up to the holiday on Monday, Sept. 7.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Are Labor Day sales worth it?Labor Day has traditionally been a good time to find deals in many categories, but whether they're worth it or not depends entirely on what you're looking for. Compared to sales like Black Friday or Prime Day, Labor Day falls short on volume and quality of discounts, but you might still find a good price on tech or kitchen appliances that will match those holiday prices—or even beat them. title: Why You Might Need to Roll Back Windows' Latest Update
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 31, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: NguyenDucQuang via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Microsoft's latest Windows update comes with cool new features that users have been asking for. Unfortunately, it comes with glaring bugs as well.
                                            The update makes it possible to move and resize the task bar, and introduces improvements to Windows Search.
                                            At the same time, it breaks the cursor, hiding it entirely or making it too small or large. In addition, your wallpaper may disappear, and fonts may be blurry.
                                            The only workaround at this time is uninstalling the latest update, which luckily isn't difficult or dangerous to do.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're the kind of person who installs Windows updates as soon as they hit your PC, you're likely running version KB5120998 of Windows 11 right now. Microsoft released it on Thursday, and while it's an optional update, it isn't locked behind its Windows Insider program. As such, anyone who has manually checked for new updates since then will have seen it, and could have installed it. Unfortunately, that might have been a mistake.
As reported by Windows Insider, the latest Windows 11 update is a big one. It includes some major updates to Windows customization, including changes that Microsoft has been testing for months. For example, the update lets you move and resize the taskbar however you like, and there are other changes that improve Windows Search for the better. These updates have previouly been exclusive to Insiders, but are now officially part of Windows 11. But it's not all good news.Windows 11's latest update is buggyIn addition to these new features, it seems Microsoft inadvertently shipped some bugs with this update. Perhaps the most impactful of them, and the one most users will notice right away, is an issue where the cursor doesn't appear onscreen—or, when it does, it appears too big or too small. Some users report their cursors are enormous, while others find them annoyingly small. Unless you use your keyboard to control everything on your PC, losing access to your cursor isn't really an option, and even inconsistent UI experiences aren't really acceptable in 2026, considering Windows has had a cursor since 1985.
Luckily, Microsoft has a fix in the works. The company formally addressed the bug on a support page, stating, "Microsoft has received reports indicating that mouse cursor personalization settings are being changed or reverted to certain standard settings. This occurs following installation of Windows updates released August 27 2026 (KB5120998) and later."It's not just the cursor causing issues, though. Following this update, Windows may forget your wallpaper settings, so your desktop appears black. You can bring your wallpaper back, but this glitch may occur every time you restart your PC. There are also reports that some fonts appear blurry, which would be particularly annoying on high-resolution displays. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
If you're experiencing any or all of these bugs, the only solution at this time appears to be rolling back the update. As Windows Latest highlights, users did see their cursors return to normal following the rollback, and those specific wallpaper glitches were only reported with this latest version. Luckily, it isn't too difficult to uninstall a recent Windows update. To do so, head to Settings > Windows Update > Update History > Uninstall. Here, find the update (KB5120998), then choose "Uninstall." Windows Latest notes that because this update was optional, you won't lose any security patches this way. Hopefully, Windows' next update is a bit more stable than this one.

schema.headline: Why You Might Need to Roll Back Windows' Latest Update
